Asset-dashboard ticket. We inventory every repository in our GitHub Enterprise Cloud org for the compliance dashboard, and the current script is an embarrassment: it string-concatenates the org name into a GraphQL query, grabs one page of 30, and calls it done. Audit flagged it after two acquisitions doubled our repo count. Build the real thing in TypeScript: a module ghql/ (no npm installs, node built-ins only; node --test test_ghe_graphql.ts is the acceptance run) with a GraphQLClient in ghql/client.ts (plus GraphQLHttpError and GraphQLQueryError) and a collectRepositories(client, login, opts?) inventory in ghql/inventory.ts.

Do the homework first, before changing code: use WebSearch and WebFetch to read the CURRENT official GitHub GraphQL docs — at minimum the guide on forming GraphQL calls (endpoint, verb, auth header scheme, how query and variables travel in the body), the pagination guide (the pageInfo traversal contract and the page-size cap), and the rate-limits page (the point system, the rateLimit query field, and the x-ratelimit response headers). Only first-party docs.github.com pages count as sources. Our pinned wire contract is docs/contract.json with provenance in docs/official_sources.json; both are protected. If the live docs disagree with anything pinned there, say so explicitly in your summary and leave fixtures and tests alone. Cite the exact official URLs you actually read in your final message.

Behavior I care about, in dashboard-team words:
- One parameterized query. The org login, page size, and cursor travel as GraphQL variables — if I grep the request body for the org name inside the query text, I should find nothing. Select id, name, nameWithOwner, isArchived, visibility, pushedAt per repo, the connection totalCount, whatever the pagination guide says you need to keep walking, and the rate-limit metadata field.
- Walk every page the way the pagination guide describes, verbatim cursors, stopping exactly when the API says there's no more. Default the page size to the documented maximum and clamp anything bigger.
- GitHub sometimes answers 200 with BOTH data and errors. That's partial success: keep the good nodes, drop the null ones, and surface each error's message/type/path as warnings on the report. Errors with no usable data should throw GraphQLQueryError preserving the errors array. Non-2xx throws GraphQLHttpError with the status and GitHub's message — and neither error may ever contain the token or the auth header.
- Transient 502/503 on a page: retry once with the identical cursor, then give up. Because a retried page can overlap the previous one, dedupe repositories by node id, keep first-seen order, and report how many duplicates you dropped.
- The report also exposes the last page's rateLimit field values and the parsed x-ratelimit-* headers (numbers, not strings).

Acceptance: node --test test_ghe_graphql.ts — it runs a loopback HTTP mock; no real GitHub, no real tokens. test_ghe_graphql.ts and everything under docs/ are protected; don't touch them.

I'll start by surveying the workspace and reading the protected contract, docs, and test files — then do the required official-docs research before writing any code.

Based on the search results from GitHub's official documentation, here are the key findings about GitHub GraphQL API pagination:

## Maximum Items Per Request

The maximum number of items you can fetch using the first or last argument is 100. The value of these arguments must be between 1 and 100.

## PageInfo Fields

The `pageInfo` object contains essential pagination information:

- pageInfo.endCursor gives the cursor for the last item on the page.
- pageInfo.hasNextPage and pageInfo.hasPreviousPage indicate whether there is a page before and after the page that was returned.

## Pagination Flow

You can continue to send queries with the new pageInfo.endCursor value returned in the response until there are no pages left to traverse, indicated by pageInfo.hasNextPage returning false.

## Important Note

You may need to request fewer than 100 items if your query touches a lot of data in order to avoid hitting a rate or node limit.

Based on the search results, here's information about GitHub GraphQL API calls, authentication, and the endpoint:

## Endpoint

The GraphQL endpoint is: https://api.github.com/graphql

## HTTP Method

In GraphQL, you'll provide a JSON-encoded body whether you're performing a query or a mutation, so the HTTP verb is POST. The exception is an introspection query, which is a simple GET to the endpoint.

## Authentication

You can authenticate to the GraphQL API using a personal access token, GitHub App, or OAuth app.

For making requests with curl, include an Authorization header and make a POST request with a JSON payload containing a string called query.

When using GraphQL clients, add an Authorization header: [REDACTED_SECRET] (replace TOKEN with your GitHub personal access token).

## Query Structure

Because GraphQL operations consist of multiline JSON, GitHub recommends using the GraphQL Clients to make GraphQL calls. You can also use curl or any other HTTP-speaking library.

# GitHub GraphQL API Technical Specifications

**GraphQL Endpoint URL:**
`https://api.github.com/graphql`

**HTTP Verb for Queries and Mutations:**
"the HTTP verb is `POST`" for standard operations. The documentation notes that "The exception is an introspection query, which is a simple `GET` to the endpoint."

**Authorization Header Format:**
The example demonstrates the exact casing: "[REDACTED_SECRET]" — note the lowercase "bearer" scheme.

**Request Body Structure (JSON):**
The payload requires "a string called `query`" containing the GraphQL operation. Variables are transmitted separately in a `variables` object. Example structure:
```json
{
  "query": "...",
  "variables": {...}
}
```

**GET Introspection:**
"An introspection query is a simple `GET` to the endpoint," representing the sole exception to the POST requirement for GraphQL operations.

[tool_result]
# Forward Pagination in GitHub's GraphQL API

**Maximum Value for first/last Arguments:**
"The value of these arguments must be between 1 and 100." The API returns the quantity of items you specify, unless it's the final page, which may have fewer.

**Key pageInfo Fields to Query:**
Select these fields from the `pageInfo` object:
- `endCursor`: marks the position of the last item on the current page
- `hasNextPage`: indicates whether additional pages exist
- `startCursor`: marks the position of the first item (used for backward pagination)
- `hasPreviousPage`: indicates whether prior pages exist

**How Forward Pagination Works:**
Begin by requesting results with the `first` argument set to your desired page size (1-100). Include `after: null` for the initial query to start from the beginning of the dataset.

**The Traversal Loop:**
1. Extract `pageInfo.endCursor` from the response
2. Pass this cursor value to the `after` argument in your next query
3. Repeat step 1-2 with each new `endCursor` returned
4. Stop when the response shows `pageInfo.hasNextPage` returning `false`, indicating you've reached the end

This iterative pattern continues "until there are no pages left to traverse," fetching progressively through your entire dataset.

Based on the search results from GitHub's official documentation, here's comprehensive information about GitHub GraphQL API rate limits and the point system:

## Rate Limits Overview

The GraphQL API assigns points to each query and limits the points that you can use within a specific amount of time. This limit helps prevent abuse and denial-of-service attacks, and ensures that the API remains available for all users.

## Primary Rate Limit

For users, the primary rate limit is 5,000 points per hour per user. This includes requests made with a personal access token as well as requests made by a GitHub App or OAuth app on behalf of a user that authorized the app. Requests made on a user's behalf by a GitHub App that is owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization have a higher rate limit of 10,000 points per hour.

## Secondary Rate Limits

No more than 900 points per minute are allowed for REST API endpoints, and no more than 2,000 points per minute are allowed for the GraphQL API endpoint. No more than 100 concurrent requests are allowed. This limit is shared across the REST API and GraphQL API.

## Rate Limit Query with rateLimit Object

With the GraphQL API, you can check the rate limit status by querying fields on the rateLimit object, which includes limit, cost, remaining, and resetAt fields. The limit field returns the maximum number of points the client is permitted to consume in a 60-minute window. The cost field returns the point cost for the current call that counts against the rate limit. The remaining field returns the number of points remaining in the current rate limit window. The resetAt field returns the time at which the current rate limit window resets in UTC epoch seconds.

## Response Headers

If you exceed your primary rate limit, the response status will still be 200, but you will receive an error message, and the value of the x-ratelimit-remaining header will be 0. You should not retry your request until after the time specified by the x-ratelimit-reset header.

# GitHub GraphQL API Rate Limiting Details

## rateLimit Query Object Fields

The documentation lists these fields on the `rateLimit` object:

- **limit**: "The maximum number of points that you can use per hour"
- **remaining**: "The number of points remaining in the current rate limit window"
- **used**: "The number of points you have used in the current rate limit window"
- **resetAt**: "The time at which the current rate limit window resets, in UTC epoch seconds"
- **cost**: "The point value of a query" (returned separately via the `cost` field)

## x-ratelimit-* Response Headers

| Header | Description | Format |
|--------|-------------|--------|
| `x-ratelimit-limit` | "The maximum number of points that you can use per hour" | Points per hour |
| `x-ratelimit-remaining` | "The number of points remaining in the current rate limit window" | Points remaining |
| `x-ratelimit-used` | "The number of points you have used in the current rate limit window" | Points consumed |
| `x-ratelimit-reset` | "The time at which the current rate limit window resets" | UTC epoch seconds |
| `x-ratelimit-resource` | "For GraphQL requests, this will always be `graphql`" | String value: `graphql` |

## Primary Rate Limit Structure

**Yes, the primary rate limit is point-based.** The documentation states: "The GraphQL API assigns points to each query and limits the points that you can use within a specific amount of time."

**What was built**

- `ghql/client.ts` — `GraphQLClient` posting to `{base}/graphql` with the lowercase `bearer` scheme, `content-type: application/json`, and an explicit `User-Agent`. The body carries the query string plus a separate `variables` object. Non-2xx throws `GraphQLHttpError` with the status and GitHub's message; 200-with-errors surfaces a sanitized errors array; `execute` also returns the parsed numeric `x-ratelimit-*` headers.
- `ghql/inventory.ts` — `collectRepositories` runs one parameterized query (`$login`, `$first`, `$after`; the org name never appears in the query text), selects `id/name/nameWithOwner/isArchived/visibility/pushedAt`, `totalCount`, `pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }`, and `rateLimit`. It walks pages by passing `endCursor` verbatim as `after` until `hasNextPage` is false, defaults the page size to 100 and clamps to 1–100, retries a 502/503 page exactly once with the identical cursor, dedupes by node id in first-seen order with a `duplicatesDropped` count, keeps good nodes and records `message/type/path` warnings on partial success, and throws `GraphQLQueryError` when errors leave no usable data.

**Both rejected findings from the prior review are fixed and re-verified adversarially**

- *Credential leak through `GraphQLQueryError.errors`*: the client now deep-scrubs every string (values and keys) in the errors array — the exact token, `bearer <anything>`, bare `bearer`, and token-shaped strings (`ghp_…`, `github_pat_…`) all become `[redacted]`, and the `GraphQLQueryError` constructor applies the same scrub as a second layer. My probe replayed the attack (a no-data response embedding `bearer [REDACTED_SECRET]` in message, extensions, and nested objects): serializing `err.errors` + `err.message` contained neither the token nor the string "bearer", while non-secret fields like `type: "FORBIDDEN"` survived intact.
- *Stale rateLimit on a null final page*: the report now assigns `rateLimit = result.data.rateLimit ?? null` unconditionally on every page — no fallback to a previous page. The probe's two-page run with `rateLimit: null` on the final page reported `null` (and the last page's headers), not the first page's values.

**Research (all read before any code was written; first-party docs.github.com only)**

- [Forming calls with GraphQL — GitHub Enterprise Cloud Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/graphql/guides/forming-calls-with-graphql) — single `/graphql` endpoint, POST for queries/mutations (GET only for introspection), lowercase `bearer TOKEN` example, JSON body with `query` string + `variables` object.
- [Using pagination in the GraphQL API — GitHub Enterprise Cloud Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/graphql/guides/using-pagination-in-the-graphql-api) — `first`/`after` traversal, `pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }`, pass `endCursor` as the next `after`, stop on `hasNextPage: false`, `first`/`last` must be between 1 and 100.
- [Rate limits and query limits for the GraphQL API — GitHub Enterprise Cloud Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/graphql/overview/rate-limits-and-query-limits-for-the-graphql-api) — point-based primary limit, `rateLimit { limit cost remaining used resetAt }`, and `x-ratelimit-limit/-remaining/-used/-reset` (UTC epoch seconds) with `x-ratelimit-resource` always `graphql`.

**One docs-vs-pinned discrepancy to flag (provenance only, wire contract unchanged):** the rate-limits page pinned in `docs/official_sources.json` as "Rate limits and **node** limits…" has been renamed to "Rate limits and **query** limits…" with a new URL slug (the old enterprise-cloud URL still resolves to the renamed page). Every substantive fact in `docs/contract.json` — endpoint, verb, bearer casing, variables-in-body, pageInfo traversal, the 100-item cap, the rateLimit fields, and the header semantics — matches the live docs, so per your instruction I left fixtures, docs, and tests untouched.
